records.name: Charles Francis Adams
records.bio: Adams appears in the Auckland procurement chain as the person who physically delivered Ward-linked Blaschka models in 1885. A triangular settlement also connected Auckland, Adams and Ward, so the project treats him as a preparator and delivery actor rather than as maker or seller.

records.name: Alfred William Alcock
records.bio: Alfred William Alcock was superintendent of the Indian Museum in Calcutta. An official 1894 guide signed by him documents the Invertebrate Gallery and its glass-model displays, linking a named museum administrator to the later display history of a verified Blaschka customer.

records.name: Frank Collins Baker
records.bio: Baker was an American malacologist whose early twentieth-century work intersects the documented history of the Museo Nacional de México Blaschka collection. His record helps connect later zoological study and museum documentation to a collection acquired decades earlier.

records.name: P. T. Barnum
records.bio: Tufts archival research states that Barnum purchased Blaschka sea creatures in 1885 for exhibition in the Barnum Museum of Natural History. The purchase year, purchaser and purpose are strong; the exact model count, price and dealer route remain open.
records.open: The exact model count, price and dealer route for the 1885 Tufts purchase remain unresolved.

records.name: Louis C. Bierweiler
records.bio: Bierweiler was a Harvard-associated curator whose 1931 European journey included a documented visit to Rudolf Blaschka at Hosterwitz. His surviving travel diary, notes, receipts, ephemera and photographs offer an unusually continuous later view of the workshop and its institutional visitors.

records.name: Joseph William Blankinship
records.bio: Blankinship was a botanist and Rudolf Blaschka’s field companion during the 1895 United States journey. His place in the project is tied to the second American field campaign and the movement of botanical observations and material back toward the workshop.

records.name: Karolina Blaschka
records.bio: Karolina is visible in the surviving archive as part of the workshop household and, more cautiously, its knowledge infrastructure. Family papers and correspondence place her inside Rudolf’s working and visitor world, but the present evidence does not justify attributing model making or scientific authorship to her.
records.open: Extent of her recurrent role in workshop visitors, correspondence and knowledge mediation beyond the documented household evidence.

records.name: Leopold Blaschka
records.bio: Leopold moved from the family glass trade into scientific model making in the 1860s. Early botanical work, sea-anemone models and later zoological catalogues turned the Dresden workshop into an international supplier of study objects; this project follows the observation, making, cataloguing and commercial records around that work.

records.name: Rudolf Blaschka
records.bio: Rudolf joined the workshop in the 1870s and increasingly carried its scientific and technical work. His 1892 and 1895 American field trips connected botanical observation, collecting and drawing to work in Hosterwitz, and after Leopold’s death he continued the Harvard botanical commission.

records.name: John Wesley Carr
records.bio: Carr directed Nottingham’s municipal Natural History Museum while teaching natural sciences at University College Nottingham. Workshop correspondence shows him trying to deal directly with Hosterwitz, but the British agency arrangement with Damon constrained that route.

records.name: Thomas Frederick Cheeseman
records.bio: Cheeseman’s long correspondence with Ward makes Auckland one of the clearest museum-side procurement stories in the project. He requested a priced catalogue, asked for samples before a larger commitment, worked within a restricted cash budget and repeatedly considered a much larger order that never materialised.

records.name: Robert Damon
records.bio: Workshop correspondence places Damon at the centre of British and Irish sales. An agency arrangement and later letters show him coordinating orders, advance payments and institutional delivery, while also constraining direct museum-to-Hosterwitz dealing in cases such as Nottingham.

records.name: John William Dawson
records.bio: Dawson was a geologist and university principal at McGill whose correspondence with Henry Augustus Ward places him in the wider acquisition network for natural-history teaching objects. His record is retained where the Blaschka backend can connect that institutional context to the object trade.

records.name: William Buck Dwight
records.bio: Dwight was Professor of Natural History and curator of Vassar’s museum during the 1887 purchase of Blaschka invertebrate models. His institutional position is secure, but the surviving evidence does not yet prove that he personally placed or paid for the order.
records.open: Who placed and paid for the Vassar purchase in 1887 remains unresolved at person level.

records.name: Karl Eggerth senior
records.bio: Karl Eggerth senior appears as buyer and donor in the documented provenance chain from the Blaschka workshop through Václav Frič to Kremsmünster. His record is intentionally narrow and follows the transaction and donation evidence rather than supplying a speculative general biography.

records.name: Theodor Eimer
records.bio: Eimer was a zoologist and Tübingen professor associated with the acquisition and teaching use of Blaschka models. His record belongs to the university-side history of how catalogue models entered zoological instruction.

records.name: Antonín Frič
records.bio: Antonín Frič was a zoologist and museum curator in Prague. He appears in the National Museum environment connected with Blaschka models and with the wider Frič family natural-history business.

records.name: Václav Frič
records.bio: Frič built a Prague natural-history business that became an important retail and distribution route for scientific specimens and Blaschka glass invertebrates. In this project he is treated as a commercial intermediary whose catalogues, sales and institutional connections carried workshop objects into Central European and other collections.

records.name: William F. Ganong
records.bio: Ganong was a botanist and Rudolf Blaschka’s field companion during the 1892 United States journey. Letters, specimens and travel records make him a key link between field observation in North America and the botanical work later carried out in Hosterwitz.

records.name: Alexander Goette
records.bio: Goette was a zoologist and university professor documented as an intermediary for Strasbourg’s 1890 order of Blaschka models. His record links institutional selection and commissioning to a specific university teaching collection.

records.name: George Lincoln Goodale
records.bio: Goodale, founding director of Harvard’s Botanical Museum, negotiated the botanical commission with Leopold and Rudolf. In this network he is both commissioner and scientific mediator, translating museum teaching needs into a sustained workshop programme.

records.name: Philip Henry Gosse
records.bio: Gosse’s published marine zoology, especially his richly illustrated work on sea anemones, belongs to the visual and scientific source environment of early Blaschka zoological models. He is included here as a source-author rather than as a documented buyer or workshop correspondent.

records.name: Albert C. L. G. Günther
records.bio: Günther was a zoologist at the British Museum and appears in the museum-side history of Blaschka holdings. The project uses his record to connect departmental custody, correspondence and collection administration rather than treating the museum as a single impersonal recipient.

records.name: Julius von Haast
records.bio: Haast, geologist and director of Canterbury Museum, appears in the Australasian correspondence and collection network surrounding Blaschka models. His inclusion here follows documented institutional and commercial links rather than general scientific acquaintance.

records.name: Ernst Haeckel
records.bio: Haeckel’s published zoological descriptions and illustrations form part of the scientific and visual environment against which some Blaschka model designs can be studied. He is included as a source-author; the project does not turn that published relationship into an undocumented personal collaboration.

records.name: James Hector
records.bio: Hector was a scientist and museum director in New Zealand whose correspondence intersects the Otago and Hutton collection network. In the People index he functions as an institutional node within the broader Australasian circulation of natural-history objects.

records.name: Thomas Holbein Hendley
records.bio: Hendley, a surgeon and museum organiser in Jaipur, was the honorary secretary and order organiser in the 1886–1887 Jeypore Blaschka transaction. Workshop correspondence lets the project follow his order through manufacture, payment, cases and the Trieste–Bombay route.

records.name: Alfonso L. Herrera
records.bio: Herrera was a Mexican biologist and naturalist whose institutional work belongs to the succession history of the Mexico City Blaschka collection. He is included where museum reorganisation and scientific administration affect how the surviving objects can be traced.

records.name: Rev. Henry H. Higgins
records.bio: Higgins had organised Liverpool’s invertebrate collections and chaired its Museum Sub-Committee. The 1887 workshop dispatch names a Higgins as recipient; contextual identification with Henry H. Higgins is strong but remains qualified because the surviving workshop text is OCR-corrupted.
records.open: The OCR-corrupted recipient in the 1887 Liverpool dispatch is strongly contextualised as Higgins, but the identification remains qualified.

records.name: Frederick Wollaston Hutton
records.bio: Hutton, a zoologist and museum curator in New Zealand, appears in correspondence concerning Blaschka models and comparative collections. His records help connect museum-side selection and ordering to the wider Ward and Australasian network.

records.name: Stephen Koob
records.bio: Koob’s work connects modern glass conservation directly to object biography. Corning conserved the Tufts models recovered from loan custody, and Vassar separately records an arrangement with him to repair and restore its Blaschka invertebrates.

records.name: E. Ray Lankester
records.bio: Lankester was a zoologist and university professor associated with the UCL teaching collection. The backend preserves a distinct 1890 Lankester catalogue and provenance layer, making him an important bridge between teaching practice, collection formation and surviving models.

records.name: Archibald Liversidge
records.bio: Liversidge was a chemist, university scientist and Australian Museum trustee whose correspondence and institutional work intersect the procurement network for scientific teaching collections. The project tracks him as a museum- and university-side intermediary rather than as a Blaschka dealer.

records.name: Godefroy Lunel
records.bio: Lunel was the first director of Geneva’s natural-history museum and is named as the recipient in the 1888 Blaschka acquisition and shipment history. His record anchors the person-level side of an otherwise institutional transaction.

records.name: Madho Singh II of Jaipur
records.bio: Madho Singh II was the ruler of Jaipur and the royal patron in the institutional setting of the Jeypore and Albert Hall Museum collections. His record represents the patronage and museum-building context around the 1886–1887 Blaschka order rather than a claim that he personally selected individual models.

records.name: Pietro Marchi
records.bio: The Florence evidence identifies Marchi as the architect of a systematic teaching collection assembled through multiple purchases. He selected catalogue models and built a local sequence that eventually numbered 118 objects; the evidence does not require that he personally made every payment or received every shipment.

records.name: Philip Brookes Mason
records.bio: Mason was a physician, naturalist and major private collector at Burton-on-Trent. His collection included Blaschka models and later dispersed, making him important for tracing how privately assembled scientific collections entered later museum histories.

records.name: Andrew McClellan
records.bio: In 2006 McClellan rediscovered Tufts archival correspondence that pointed back to Corning custody. That documentary find reopened a collection thought to have been destroyed in the 1975 Barnum Hall fire and led to the 2007 return of ten models.

records.name: Frederick McCoy
records.bio: McCoy was a naturalist and founding museum director in Melbourne. One acquisition hypothesis links him and Henry Ward to the Melbourne Blaschka models, but the project keeps that route open until the person-level transaction evidence can be closed.
records.open: The exact transaction route by which the Melbourne collection was acquired remains unresolved.

records.name: Paul Perrot
records.bio: Perrot, a director of the Corning Museum of Glass, appears in later loan and custody histories of Blaschka collections. The project retains his record while distinguishing the general institutional role from individual object-level decisions that still require file-level confirmation.
records.open: His precise role in individual Blaschka loans and custody decisions remains to be resolved from institutional files.

records.name: Isabelle Pirotte
records.bio: Pirotte is a conservator-restorer associated with the 2008 treatment of the Geneva Blaschka collection. Her record belongs to the later material history of the models, where conservation becomes part of provenance rather than an afterthought.

records.name: Ludwig Reichenbach
records.bio: As director of Dresden’s natural-history museum and botanical garden, Reichenbach helped place Leopold’s early glass work in a scientific museum setting. His role is therefore institutional as well as personal: he belongs to the early chain through which modelling moved from private patronage toward public scientific display.

records.name: Henri Reiling
records.bio: Reiling is a modern scholar whose cataloguing and collection research has been repeatedly used to identify, compare and reconstruct surviving Blaschka holdings. His work forms part of the project’s research history and source genealogy.

records.name: Emmanuel G. Reynaud
records.bio: Reynaud is a researcher involved in reconstructing Irish Blaschka collection histories and later digital work around surviving holdings. His record marks the modern research network through which dispersed collections are being reidentified and connected.

records.name: Stuart Oliver Ridley
records.bio: Ridley was a zoologist in the British Museum’s Department of Zoology and appears in the institutional context of Blaschka collection records. The broader museum connection is secure, while the exact person-specific transaction role remains under review.
records.open: Person-specific transaction documentation for the British Museum Blaschka holdings remains incomplete.

records.name: Prince Camille de Rohan
records.bio: Rohan encountered Leopold’s early botanical work, commissioned a large group of exotic flower models and supported further botanical study. He also connected Leopold with Ludwig Reichenbach, helping move the work from private patronage into a public scientific setting.

records.name: Franz Eilhard Schulze
records.bio: Schulze was a zoologist whose sponge research, publications, proofs and advice intersect the workshop’s developmental and anatomical modelling. He is one of the clearest cases in which scientific collaboration can be followed alongside the objects themselves.

records.name: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson
records.bio: D’Arcy Thompson was a zoologist and teacher central to the Dundee teaching collection and its later provenance. His record connects classroom use, collection history and the later imaging and interpretation of surviving Blaschka models.

records.name: G. W. Tryon
records.bio: George Washington Tryon Jr. was a malacologist and curator at the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia. He belongs to the institutional setting in which Blaschka objects were acquired, while the exact person-specific acquisition correspondence remains a research target.
records.open: Person-specific Philadelphia acquisition correspondence has not yet been recovered.

records.name: Édouard Van Beneden
records.bio: Van Beneden was a zoologist at Liège linked to the university’s 1886 direct catalogue-based commission from the Blaschka workshop. He is treated as a museum- and university-side commissioner in a documented acquisition chain.

records.name: Henry Augustus Ward
records.bio: Ward’s Natural Science Establishment connected the Blaschka workshop to museums and teaching collections, especially in North America and Australasia. The Auckland case shows catalogue circulation, exchange, samples, prices and settlement moving through Ward; the project does not assume that every American acquisition followed his route.

records.name: Mary Lee Ware
records.bio: Mary Lee Ware was the principal sponsor and an important correspondent in the Harvard botanical commission. The project treats her patronage as infrastructure: long-term funding, communication and trust made the later workshop programme possible.

records.name: Henry Woodward
records.bio: Woodward was a British Museum geologist and museum official whose name appears in the institutional history surrounding Blaschka holdings. His record helps disaggregate the people who handled scientific collections inside large museums.

records.name: Patricia Egan
records.bio: Egan’s Australian Museum research reconstructed the acquisition and later identification history of its Blaschka models from trustees’ records, outward correspondence, surviving labels and catalogue comparison. She also participated in the 2009 object-identification work that matched most surviving models to historical catalogue entries.

records.name: Agathe Petit
records.bio: Petit studied and treated a damaged Strasbourg Blaschka cephalopod as part of a conservation-restoration project. Her work also contributes to the recent condition history of the Strasbourg collection and its preparation for renewed display.

records.name: John Henry Comstock
records.bio: Comstock appears in the Cornell-side acquisition network through professional correspondence with Henry Augustus Ward in 1885. The surviving Ward correspondence makes him a named institutional actor in the environment from which Cornell’s Blaschka collection emerged.
records.open: The surviving correspondence should still be separated carefully from any object-by-object purchasing attribution.

records.name: Eric Callaghan
records.bio: Callaghan co-authored the archival reconstruction of the University College Dublin collection and the later national survey of Blaschka invertebrate models in Irish institutions. That work connects order books, invoices, museum registers, transfers and surviving objects.

records.name: Chris Meechan
records.bio: Meechan appears in the Australian Museum’s modern identification history and in the wider Blaschka literature. In 2009 he worked with Patricia Egan and Michela Mitchell to compare underside numbers and published zoological illustrations against the historical catalogue sequence.

records.name: Gertrude Hofmeister
records.bio: Hofmeister authored an early dedicated study of the Kremsmünster glass-model collection in 1982. The article is an important bibliographic and provenance waypoint for a collection whose commercial route runs through Václav Frič and the Eggerth donation.
records.open: The full 1982 article and any object-level list cited there remain to be recovered.

records.name: Mathias Weis
records.bio: Weis publicly identified sixty-one Blaschka glass models in the collections of Stift Seitenstetten during the current collections-science project. His work is central to the project’s recent rediscovery and inventory history.
records.open: Object-level identifiers and catalogue-number crosswalks for the sixty-one models remain to be recovered publicly.

records.name: David Whitehouse
records.bio: Whitehouse’s 1991 Corning inquiry helped reopen the identification history of the Leeds sea-anemone models. Correspondence and photographs contributed to recognizing the early group as Blaschka workshop products rather than leaving the older Frič attribution unexamined.

records.name: Joan P. Jass
records.roles: invertebrate zoology curator · Milwaukee Public Museum
records.bio: Jass carried out a museum-specific comparison of Milwaukee’s Blaschka material against Ward’s 1888 catalogue in 1987. The project treats that work as the strongest known item-list lead for the Milwaukee collection even though the underlying comparison has not yet been recovered.
records.open: The 1987 item-level comparison itself remains unrecovered.

records.name: Drew Harvell
records.bio: Harvell helped bring Cornell’s Blaschka invertebrates back into scientific and public use through research, teaching and digital documentation. A 2016 Cornell project with Nelson Hairston explicitly aimed to expand the online collection for interdisciplinary teaching and access.

records.name: Hazel J. Doyle
records.bio: Doyle co-authored both the University College Dublin collection reconstruction and the later survey of Blaschka models across Irish institutions. The studies combine archival order evidence with later museum registers, condition data and collection movements.

records.name: Federigo Federighi
records.bio: Federighi’s openly licensed photograph documents a group of Blaschka cnidarian models at the Natural History Museum of Pisa University. The project includes him as a modern documentation actor because the image provides a verifiable public visual anchor for the collection.

records.name: Holly Daws
records.bio: Daws is named in National Museums Scotland’s conservation account of a damaged Blaschka model. The treatment record makes her part of the objects’ later material biography, documenting cleaning, stabilization, support making, colour matching and rebonding.

records.name: C. Giles Miller
records.roles: museum scientist · Natural History Museum collection historian
records.bio: Miller co-authored the principal published inventory and collection history of the Natural History Museum’s Blaschka holdings. The study is a central reference for acquisition, survival and object-level reconstruction in the London collection.

records.name: Miranda Lowe
records.roles: museum scientist · collection historian · object authentication
records.bio: Lowe co-authored the Natural History Museum collection history and later appears in technical authentication work on original Blaschka components. Her record therefore joins published collection reconstruction to object-level museum expertise.

records.name: Eva Rydlová
records.bio: Rydlová co-authored the conservation and technical study of the National Museum in Prague’s surviving Blaschka octopus. The work documents damage, construction and treatment while anchoring one of the best-studied individual zoological models.

records.name: Ivana Kopecká
records.bio: Kopecká co-authored the conservation and technical study of the National Museum in Prague’s surviving Blaschka octopus. Her work contributes directly to the object’s documented construction, damage and restoration history.

records.name: John Armitage
records.bio: Armitage salvaged and carried out some restoration on the Leeds Blaschka sea-anemone models in 1959. The surviving account does not support a treatment count or object-by-object reconstruction, but it establishes a named intervention in the collection’s post-war survival history.
records.open: The number of models treated, techniques used and individual object assignments remain undocumented.

records.name: Katherine Larson
records.bio: Larson’s Corning-based research assembled a global picture of surviving Blaschka collections and historical distribution. Her 2016 account is an important modern census point for the project’s own collection-mapping work.

records.name: Helena Wouters
records.bio: Wouters is named among the IRPA analysts who examined glass, adhesives and paint layers in the Liège Blaschka collection. Her work belongs to the analytical strand of the collection’s restoration and redisplay project.

records.name: Marina Van Bos
records.bio: Van Bos is named among the IRPA analysts who examined glass, adhesives and paint layers in the Liège Blaschka collection. The analysis forms part of the evidence base for the collection’s conservation and exhibition history.

records.name: Andrew Dickson White
records.bio: White’s papers form one of the archival contexts through which Cornell’s early natural-history collecting and institutional networks can be reconstructed. The project keeps him as an institutional actor where Blaschka-related correspondence or collection formation intersects that archive.
records.open: His precise object-level role in Cornell’s Blaschka acquisitions should be distinguished from the broader institutional context preserved in his papers.

records.name: Louis Agassiz
records.roles: zoologist · Harvard museum founder · Ward correspondent
records.bio: A surviving 1869 letter from Henry Augustus Ward to Agassiz places the Museum of Comparative Zoology founder in the early Ward–Harvard institutional network. The finding-aid evidence establishes correspondence but does not by itself prove that this particular letter concerned Blaschka models.
records.open: The 1869 Ward–Agassiz letter still requires content-level verification before it can be treated as Blaschka correspondence.

records.name: Elizabeth Hodges Clark
records.roles: Harvard museum worker · receiving and inspection
records.bio: Harvard historical interpretation identifies Clark as likely assisting with unpacking and inspecting Blaschka invertebrates and flowers. The project retains that labour history while marking the attribution as institutional interpretation rather than item-level documentary proof.
records.open: The unpacking and inspection role is probable rather than object-by-object documented.

records.name: Jan Brazier
records.bio: Brazier co-authored the reconstruction of model and wall-chart circulation for teaching biology in Australia and New Zealand. The study is especially useful for the Frič–Liversidge network, museum consignments and the later University of Sydney teaching loan.

records.name: Molly Duggins
records.bio: Duggins co-authored the reconstruction of teaching models and wall charts in Australia and New Zealand. Her work supplies a broader material and educational context for the Blaschka models entering Australasian museums through Frič and related dealers.

records.name: Deborah White
records.roles: museum writer · Australian Museum conservation history
records.bio: White documented the restoration challenges surrounding the Australian Museum’s Blaschka sea anemones and their return to display in March 2010 after many decades. Her account provides an institutional anchor for the collection’s recent material history.

records.name: W. J. Stephens
records.roles: university scientist · Australian Museum loan actor
records.bio: Stephens appears in the 1884 transfer of the Frič teaching collection from the Australian Museum to the University of Sydney for lecture use. The wider collection context is relevant to Blaschka circulation, although the surviving evidence does not isolate which Blaschka objects, if any, were included in that particular loan.
records.open: The Blaschka object scope of the 1884 loan remains unresolved.

records.name: Michela Mitchell
records.bio: Mitchell participated in the Australian Museum’s 2009 identification campaign with Patricia Egan and Chris Meechan. The team compared underside number stickers with the 1871 catalogue and published zoological illustrations, identifying all but one surviving model.

records.name: Sabine Hackethal
records.bio: Hackethal authored the institutional history used to reconstruct the Berlin Blaschka collection: its acquisition scale, surviving pieces, present locations, Schulze collaboration and continuing teaching use. The account accompanied the 2012 Berlin exhibition.

records.name: Sarah Kemp
records.bio: Kemp authored the 2012 finding aid for the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia’s Blaschka glass models. That record preserves collection extent, historical counts, original components, condition problems, provenance and the 2012 rehousing and display history.

records.name: Geoffrey N. Swinney
records.roles: museum curator · National Museums Scotland collection historian
records.bio: Swinney reconstructed the history of the Blaschka models in National Museums Scotland, including the large nineteenth-century acquisitions and institutional succession of the collection. His study is the principal published anchor for the Edinburgh group.

records.name: Thomas C. Archer
records.bio: Archer directed the Edinburgh Museum of Science and Art through the 1866 and 1868 Blaschka orders. His record makes the museum’s early acquisition history legible at person level rather than leaving it as an anonymous institutional transaction.

records.name: Sarah E. Parker
records.bio: Parker’s UCL documentation is preserved in the provenance trail for individual Grant Museum Blaschka objects, including the beadlet anemone. Her work is a modern bridge between legacy collection records, teaching history and public object interpretation.

records.name: Marek Janáč
records.bio: Janáč’s 2025 article uses National Museum evidence to reconstruct the history of Prague’s surviving Blaschka octopus, including earlier display with a jellyfish model and the loss of the latter during the 1945 destruction of the museum.

records.name: Armin Laussegger
records.bio: Laussegger co-authored the collections-science report that brought the recently rediscovered Seitenstetten sea-anemone models into a wider history of the abbey’s teaching and natural-history collections. The report also links the models cautiously to Frič’s commercial range.

records.name: Sandra Sam
records.bio: Sam co-authored the 2024 Seitenstetten collections report and leads the current university project studying the abbey’s natural-history cabinet. That work provides the institutional framework for inventory, documentation and conservation of the newly identified Blaschka models.

records.name: Markus Bürscher
records.bio: Bürscher co-authored the 2026 report on the current Seitenstetten collections-science project. The report records the identification of sixty-one Blaschka models and the project’s work on inventory, documentation and conservation planning.

records.name: Theresia Hauenfels
records.bio: Hauenfels co-authored the 2026 report on research at the Seitenstetten collections-science centre. Her record connects the rediscovered Blaschka models with the broader institutional programme of inventory, documentation and conservation.

records.name: Tat'jána Spunarová
records.bio: Spunarová co-authored the major study of Václav Frič and his influence on natural-history collecting. For the Blaschka network, the article is especially important for Frič’s retailing of glass invertebrates and his catalogue-based supply to museums and teaching collections.

external.label: Journal of the History of Collections

records.name: Florian Huber
records.bio: Huber authored an object-history study devoted to Blaschka sea-anemone models. The project uses it as a comparative secondary source for early model groups and their later collection histories.
records.open: A stable open web copy or authority record has not yet been linked.

records.name: Eleonora Weixelbaumer
records.bio: Weixelbaumer is named in the current Seitenstetten project as providing conservation-restoration support, including preparatory work on Blaschka sea-anemone models. Her role makes treatment planning part of the documented rediscovery process.

records.name: Isabella Gmeindl
records.bio: Gmeindl is named in the current Seitenstetten project as providing conservation-restoration support for the natural-history collections, including preparatory work on the rediscovered Blaschka sea-anemone models.

records.name: Julia D. Sigwart
records.bio: Sigwart’s study of the Dublin Blaschka Congress provides comparative collection context and includes an object-specific Oxford anchor: an Anthea cereus model acquired in 1867 and explicitly compared with its published zoological illustration source.

records.name: Adrian Norris
records.bio: Norris’s 1995 curatorial account is the central modern source for the Leeds Blaschka models. It records the historical acquisition of sixty-four sea-anemone models, twenty-seven extant examples in 1995, war and time damage, Armitage’s salvage and the Corning-led reidentification of the group.
records.open: The 1995 count must remain a dated survival checkpoint rather than a current total.

records.name: Susan M. Rossi-Wilcox
records.roles: museum historian · Blaschka workshop and collection research
records.bio: Rossi-Wilcox examined the Leeds material and recognized the rarity and significance of its very early models. Her broader research on the Blaschkas and their lampworking practice also makes her a major modern interpreter of workshop technique and surviving collections.

records.name: Sonia Wanson
records.bio: Wanson coordinated the Liège restoration, exhibition and catalogue project and co-authored Blaschka: Maîtres et modèles. Institutional accounts also preserve her explanation of the collection’s teaching rationale and post-restoration displayability.

records.name: Jacques Ninane
records.bio: Ninane co-authored the Liège collection catalogue and is credited for object photography in the modern presentation of the collection. His work forms part of the project’s visual and publication history after conservation.

records.name: Ruthanna Dyer
records.bio: Dyer studied the educational use of Blaschka marine models in North American post-secondary institutions using Ward papers and Blaschka business records. Her work is a key synthesis for connecting the dealer network to classroom and museum use.

records.name: Rüdiger Bieler
records.bio: Bieler’s history of the Field Museum molluscan collections reconstructs the Ward’s World’s Columbian Exposition material, including Blaschka glass models, the transfer into the museum and later photographic and display anchors.

records.name: W. Barlow Ware
records.bio: Ware is documented in Cornell’s 2006 restoration, curation and display of the Blaschka marine invertebrate collection. Cornell’s object record credits his generosity, while his papers preserve a dedicated Blaschka project binder, photographs and collection material.

records.name: Nelson Hairston
records.bio: Hairston is named with Drew Harvell in Cornell’s 2016 project to expand and improve the Blaschka Glass Invertebrate Collection website for teaching and interdisciplinary access. His record belongs to the digital afterlife of the Cornell models.

records.name: Matthew D Shaw
records.bio: Shaw co-authored the 2017 Canterbury Museum study and illustrated catalogue of its Blaschka collection. The publication reconstructs acquisition and use while providing the project with a large object-level comparative catalogue.

records.name: Joanna Z Szczepanski
records.bio: Szczepanski co-authored the 2017 Canterbury Museum study and illustrated catalogue of its Blaschka collection. The work is a principal modern source for the collection’s acquisition, scientific context and surviving models.

records.name: Sarah F Murray
records.bio: Murray co-authored the 2017 Canterbury Museum study and illustrated catalogue of its Blaschka models. Her record marks the modern museum research through which the collection’s individual objects and historical setting were made publicly traceable.

records.name: Simon Hodge
records.bio: Hodge co-authored the 2017 Canterbury Museum study and illustrated catalogue. The publication combines collection history with an extensive model catalogue and is a key comparative source for the project’s Australasian network.

records.name: Cor J Vink
records.bio: Vink co-authored the 2017 Canterbury Museum study and illustrated catalogue of the museum’s Blaschka models. The work is an important modern inventory and collection-history anchor for Canterbury.

records.name: Rev. R. Henderson
records.bio: An incomplete Blaschka archive fragment is addressed to Henderson in Brighton and reports that the collection ordered by Frederick Wollaston Hutton for Otago Museum was nearly finished. The fragment places Henderson inside the communication chain but does not establish his exact function.
records.open: Henderson’s full identity, role, letter date and relationship to the Otago order remain unresolved.

records.name: Elizabeth Brill
records.bio: Brill is named in an official Museum of Comparative Zoology media record for the cleaning and conservation of Blaschka model MCZ:SC:152 in 2007. The record provides an object-level conservation event rather than only a general institutional treatment history.

records.name: Miss Washburn
records.roles: museum worker · mounting, cataloguing and labelling
records.bio: Boston Society of Natural History records place Miss Washburn in the practical labour of mounting, cataloguing and labelling zoological collections. The same reporting context includes Blaschka processing, making her one of the otherwise easily lost museum workers behind collection preparation.
records.open: Her full name and the object-level extent of her work on Blaschka models remain unidentified.

records.name: Mr. Van Vleck
records.bio: A Boston Society of Natural History annual-report context names Van Vleck with Miss Washburn in arranging and mounting zoological collections and completing Mollusca labelling and cataloguing. The record places this labour beside the Society’s Blaschka processing.
records.open: His full identity and any object-specific work on Blaschka models remain unresolved.

records.name: Giles Tillotson
records.roles: historian · Jaipur museum and exhibition history
records.bio: Tillotson’s study of the Jaipur Exhibition of 1883 supplies institutional context for Thomas Holbein Hendley, the Central Museum and its surviving acquisitions ledger. For this project it helps locate the museum-side archival route needed to close the Jeypore Blaschka order.

records.name: Seiichi Tejima
records.roles: Tokyo Educational Museum actor · catalogue and order contact
records.bio: The Tokyo module identifies Tejima with high confidence behind several corrupted archival name variants. Workshop correspondence and the delivery book connect the Tokyo Educational Museum or Educational Department to catalogues, repeated contact and a completed 1883 Blaschka shipment.
records.open: The exact object list and item-level succession from the 1883 Tokyo shipment remain to be reconstructed.

records.name: Sayaka Kobayashi
records.bio: Kobayashi co-authored a provenance study showing how Tokyo Educational Museum labels can be cross-walked to surviving Tensanbu ledger records. The study concerns a bird collection, so the project uses it as evidence for archival method and record survival rather than as proof for any Blaschka object.
records.open: Application of this ledger method to the Blaschka shipment remains a research task.

records.name: Masaru Kato
records.bio: Kato co-authored the 2020 study demonstrating how Tokyo Educational Museum provenance can be recovered through Tensanbu ledgers. The project treats the result as a methodological and archival-survival anchor, not as direct identification of Blaschka models.
records.open: Application of this ledger method to the Blaschka shipment remains a research task.

records.name: Asami Takada
records.roles: historian of instructional equipment · Tokyo Educational Museum
records.bio: Takada’s study of the Tokyo Educational Museum in the 1880s reconstructs its role in promoting and distributing scientific apparatus and specimens. That institutional history provides the teaching-equipment context for the museum’s documented contact with the Blaschka workshop.

records.name: B.J. Gill
records.bio: Gill co-authored the 2019 reconstruction of the Cheeseman–Ward correspondence and Auckland Museum exchanges. The article establishes the seven surviving Blaschka models, their catalogue numbers, prices, registration numbers and the unrealised plan for a much larger order.

records.name: H.R. Grenfell
records.bio: Grenfell co-authored the 2019 study that reconstructs Auckland Museum’s exchanges with Henry Augustus Ward. Its object-level crosswalk of seven Blaschka models is one of the project’s strongest examples of museum records, dealer correspondence and surviving objects joining cleanly.

records.name: W.M. Blom
records.bio: Blom co-authored the 2019 Auckland Museum study of the Cheeseman–Ward correspondence. The article supplies the archival and registration evidence behind the project’s seven-model Auckland provenance chain and the unfulfilled larger-order proposal.

records.name: Antonio Lazcano Araujo
records.roles: biologist · historian of the Mexico collection
records.bio: Lazcano’s account of emblematic natural-history objects in Mexico identifies surviving Blaschka models and links them to the institutional succession from the old museum at Chopo to later UNAM collections. The project uses his work as a modern collection-history anchor.

external.label: Revista de la Universidad de México

records.name: Laura Faustini
records.bio: Faustini co-authored the 2017 study of the Fondazione Scienza e Tecnica collection in Florence. The article provides the 118-object historical sequence, the 111 surviving-model count, Marchi’s role, purchase evidence, restoration history and technical-analysis results.

records.name: Stefania Lotti
records.bio: Lotti co-authored the 2017 Florence collection study that reconstructs acquisition, catalogue sequence, survival, restoration and technical analysis. It is the principal modern source behind the project’s object-level Florence module.

records.name: Helen Shaddock
records.bio: Shaddock’s 2015 collection-visit account records approximately fifty Blaschka sea-anemone models at Newcastle and describes their scientific purpose. The project retains the account as a secondary documentary checkpoint rather than an official inventory.
records.open: The reported count remains a secondary-source figure until matched to an institutional register.

records.name: Paolo Viscardi
records.bio: Viscardi’s 2019 NatSCA article provides a published Liverpool object anchor, identifying a World Museum Blaschka specimen with catalogue number 93. His wider collections work also connects the project to surviving Irish and British holdings.

records.name: Kate McNally
records.bio: McNally’s 2025 Tufts Archival Research Center account reconstructs the collection from Barnum’s 1885 purchase through Corning custody, documentary rediscovery, restoration and return. It also supplies the current archival count of twenty-two models and identifies the Biology department records behind the story.

records.name: Jonathan Heath
records.bio: Heath’s Corning Museum of Glass account reconstructs the later Tufts custody story through the 1960s correspondence, the 1972 flood, recovery of ten models, conservation and their 2007 return. The article is one of the principal institutional narratives for the case.

records.name: Helene Ragovin
records.bio: Ragovin’s 2009 Tufts account records the rediscovery and return of the university’s Blaschka models, including the Dana Laboratory closet find and Stephen Koob’s discussion of treatment. The project uses it as a contemporary institutional reconstruction with oral-history elements.

records.name: Kerstin Barndt
records.bio: Barndt co-curated the 2017 Museum of Vitreous Ecology project at Michigan. The exhibition research brought together approximately seventy-eight marine models, fragments, teaching history and the later displacement of glass models by newer visual technologies.
records.open: The proposed Harvard/Agassiz route for part of the Michigan collection remains a curatorial hypothesis rather than closed provenance.

records.name: Alice Goff
records.bio: Goff co-curated the 2017 Museum of Vitreous Ecology project at Michigan. The research documented the surviving marine models, their fragmented condition, two acquisition strata and their changing status as teaching objects and historical artifacts.
records.open: The proposed Harvard/Agassiz route for part of the Michigan collection remains a curatorial hypothesis rather than closed provenance.

records.name: R. J. Anderson
records.bio: The workshop delivery book names Anderson as buyer for two Queen’s College Galway orders: eighty-one models on 27 January 1886 and fifty-one on 19 January 1889. The two orders provide an unusually clean person-to-institution link for the Galway collection.
records.open: A fuller authority identification for R. J. Anderson remains to be added.

records.name: A. C. Haddon
records.roles: professor of zoology · Royal College of Science for Ireland buyer
records.bio: An original invoice dated 13 June 1885 records Haddon, Professor of Zoology at the Royal College of Science for Ireland, as buyer of 139 Blaschka models. The order is one of the strongest surviving Irish person-level acquisition records because the buyer, date, quantity and direct workshop route are all preserved.

records.name: Andrew Leith Adams
records.roles: professor · Queen’s College Cork acquisition actor
records.bio: Adams is the named university-side actor in the Cork collection history. A workshop draft records an earlier set already delivered and a later order of about 100 Reichsmarks to be prepared after the Dublin commissions, with Robert Damon involved in the later route.
records.open: No complete Cork order list survives in the recovered study, so the two order contents and total original model count remain unresolved.

records.name: Robert Oliver Cunningham
records.roles: professor of natural history · Belfast buyer
records.bio: Cunningham was identified in the Irish collection study as the Queen’s College Belfast professor whose Blaschka order was prepaid through Robert Damon for £8, or 160 Reichsmarks. A later workshop letter records dispatch of one box to him in Belfast.
records.open: The order list has not been located and the collection is currently unlocated; the backend preserves only an estimated original range of roughly forty-five to fifty-five models.

records.name: William Johnston Sollas
records.roles: geology professor · Trinity College Dublin buyer
records.bio: The Blaschka records identify ‘Professor Sollas’ of Trinity College Dublin as buyer of twenty-seven models on 29 April 1885: seventeen catalogue models and ten specially commissioned molluscan dissection models. Trinity’s institutional history identifies William Johnston Sollas as the geology chair of this period.

records.name: Dr Alexander Carte
records.roles: museum curator and director · Dublin acquisition context
records.bio: The Irish network reconstruction names Carte among the museum-side officials associated with the Royal Dublin Society Natural History Museum collection. The institution made repeated Blaschka purchases, and the modern study treats Carte as a likely acquisition actor while preserving the distinction between museum office and item-level ordering evidence.
records.open: The extent of Carte’s personal role in selecting, authorising or paying for individual Blaschka orders remains unresolved.

records.name: Professor Mackintosh
records.roles: Trinity College Dublin recipient · permanent-loan custody
records.bio: National Museum of Ireland registers record six Blaschka models sent on permanent loan to Professor Mackintosh at Trinity College Dublin on 4 November 1920. Four of those models were later reported on display in the TCD Zoological Museum, while label boards survive for two missing examples.
records.open: The backend does not yet establish Mackintosh’s full identity or exact institutional office.

records.name: Camil Heller
records.roles: zoologist · published source in Rudolf’s notebook
records.bio: Corning catalogue metadata for Rudolf Blaschka’s notebook Anmerkungen über Wirbellose Thiere III lists Heller as a contributor and records Heller’s work on Adriatic zoophytes and echinoderms at the head of the notebook. The project treats him as a scientific source embedded in workshop research rather than as a commercial actor.

records.name: Anna T. Jeanes
records.roles: patronage actor · Academy of Natural Sciences Philadelphia
records.bio: The Academy of Natural Sciences finding aid names Jeanes in the patronage history of its Blaschka cephalopod collection, and item 033 preserves her name on a damaged historical label. The project retains the Jeanes/Jeans spelling conflict exactly as documented.
records.open: The public finding aid does not yet expose an invoice, payment record or item-by-item accession concordance that separates patronage, selection and purchase.

records.name: Russell Carpenter
records.roles: Barnum Museum curator · Tufts/Corning loan actor
records.bio: Tufts archival research identifies Carpenter as the Barnum Museum curator who, in a 1965 letter, asked the Corning Museum of Glass to take Tufts’ Blaschka models on what the records called a permanent loan. That correspondence became crucial when the models were rediscovered and returned decades later.

records.name: Célestine Ousset
records.bio: The Strasbourg collection module identifies Ousset as the conservator-restorer responsible for Blaschka treatment during the 2023–2025 museum-renovation campaign. Her record links the historical 1890 collection directly to its current restoration and redisplay lifecycle.
records.open: Object-level treatment documentation remains a priority for future capture.

records.name: Peter Neumann
records.bio: Neumann is repeatedly credited for photographs in the Tübingen Blaschka sourcebook and object records. His images provide a substantial modern visual-documentation layer for model comparison, condition and catalogue work.

records.name: Dante Abate
records.bio: Abate took part in the 13–17 February 2017 digital-documentation campaign at the Fondazione Scienza e Tecnica in Florence. With Sorin Hermon and the Cyprus Institute, he helped document approximately fifteen Blaschka objects using object-specific 3D methods within the E-RIHS framework.
records.open: The public source does not verify that the 3D campaign was extended from the initial group to the complete collection.

records.name: Sorin Hermon
records.bio: Hermon took part in the February 2017 3D-documentation campaign at the Fondazione Scienza e Tecnica with Dante Abate and the Cyprus Institute. The project adapted documentation to differences in form, technique and glass type across approximately fifteen Blaschka objects.
records.open: The public source does not verify that the initial campaign reached the whole collection.

records.name: Carl Bento
records.bio: Bento is credited in the Australian Museum’s photographic record MA817 and in reference photography attached to Blaschka object documentation. The project keeps MA817 as a photographic or archive identifier rather than treating it automatically as a physical-object number.

records.name: James Balodimas
records.bio: Balodimas is credited for the Field Museum’s 1993 photograph of its Blaschka Tethys fimbria model, preserved under photo-archive identifier Z94040c. That image is one of the project’s direct modern anchors for the Ward and World’s Columbian Exposition collection history.
records.open: The local Field Museum inventory number and full object record remain to be linked to the photographic anchor.

records.name: Gary Hodges
records.bio: Hodges is repeatedly credited as the photographer or visual source in the Cornell-linked catalogue index used by the project. Those credits attach modern images to specific Blaschka numbers and taxa and therefore form part of the collection’s digital documentation layer.
records.open: The backend field combines photographer and source credits, so no broader photographic role is inferred beyond the credited records.

records.name: Kent Loeffler
records.bio: Loeffler is repeatedly named in the Cornell-linked catalogue index as photographer or visual source for individual Blaschka records. The project retains those credits because the images are part of the modern object-identification and comparison infrastructure.
records.open: The backend field combines photographer and source credits, so no broader role is inferred beyond the credited records.

records.name: Claire Smith
records.bio: Smith is credited as photographer or visual source for several Cornell-linked Blaschka catalogue records, including object images used in cross-collection comparison. Her record is limited to those documented image-source credits.
records.open: The backend does not yet provide a fuller authority identification for Claire Smith.

records.name: J. E. Gray
records.bio: A verified Natural History Museum archival reference records Frederick Wollaston Hutton writing to J. E. Gray on 26 July 1874. The reference places Gray in the Otago-to-British-Museum zoological network, but the contents have not yet been captured and the project does not treat the letter as Blaschka-specific correspondence.
records.open: Letter contents remain uncaptured; a Blaschka-specific connection is therefore unproven.

records.name: Robert Etheridge
records.bio: An Australian Museum archival reference records Hutton writing to Robert Etheridge on 21 August 1877. It establishes an Otago–Australian Museum exchange connection, but the letter contents have not been captured and no Blaschka-specific subject is inferred from the reference alone.
records.open: Letter contents remain uncaptured; the edge is contextual to the Otago collection network rather than proven Blaschka correspondence.
